newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Thorn boosted by payout promise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thorn boosted by payout promise.

text.p: British rentals group Thorn Plc reported flat profits on Wednesday but promised an 87 million pound ($141.9 million) sweetener for investors, boosting its shares which have fallen from favour since the firm split last year from music giant EMI.
The shares, which started life at 408 pence in August last year, have fallen steeply since the demerger from Thorn's more glamorous partner.
But the promised payout helped drive them back up from a low of 149.5 pence. They stood 5.25 pence higher at 154.5 pence by mid-session.
Pre-tax profits in the year to March 31 1997 were 171.0 million pounds, against a pro-forma 170.7 million last time. Sales rose 1.5 percent to 1.56 billion pounds from 1.53 billion.
The dividend was 13.3 pence.
Thorn, which operates Radio Rentals in Britain and Rent-a-Center in the United States, had warned in January that profits would be broadly unchanged from last year.
The profit warning, followed by British store closures and restructuring, intensified fears about Thorn's trading performance and the impact of litigation in the United States.
Chairman Sir Colin Southgate said the company had decided to return value to shareholders because of Thorn's investment needs and the strength of its financial position.
"The proposals will enhance earnings per share whilst maintaining prudent financial ratios and the flexibility to finance future growth," he said in a statement.
Finance director Steve Marshall said the share buy-back would enhance earnings per share on a proforma basis by 12 percent over a 12 month period.

Marshall said in an interview that Thorn's plans to return cash to shareholders would involve the issue of one new share for every existing Thorn ordinary share, which Thorn would then offer to buy back.

The buy-back, which will take place soon after the annual meeting in July, would reduce Thorn's shares by one seventh since the new ordinary shares would be consolidated back on a six for seven basis. Southgate said the group, which had suffered falling sales in the United States, as well as weak trading at Radio Rentals in Britain, faced a challenging year.
Marshall said Thorn was looking very hard at businesses which were not producing an acceptable return. Its Danish retail chain Fona, for example, is likely to be sold off.
He said there were also a number of other businesses in continental Europe that Thorn needed to look at from this point of view.

In Britain, Thorn is in the process of shutting 90 of its 620 Radio Rentals stores and has cut 150 jobs in a rationalisation of its central operations. Marshall said this would save about six million pounds over a 12 month period.
He said Thorn had no current plans for further restructuring, but did not rule this out depending how the business performed.

Thorn is expanding its no-frills Crazy George rental chain in Britain and plans to add around 20 to 25 outlets in the current year, including 12 in London. Longer term the group believes there is scope for 275 shops. There is one outlet in France and a second due to open there.
In the United States, which accounts for around 40 percent of group turnover, Marshall said the key aim was to drive top line sales.
Last year, the U.S. business suffered a six percent drop in same store sales in local currency terms.
Thorn has faced U.S. litigation over its rental agreements but no new cases have arisen since the group's demerger from EMI Plc last summer.
The company has made a 17.1 million pound provision against possible damages relating to a case in Minnesota. It is also facing lawsuits in Wisconsin and New Jersey. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
